issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette: Rohan still remembers the smell of burnt rubber and pavement that day his car was pulled over by a police officer. The officer's tone was aggressive, and Rohan felt a surge of fear as he tried to explain that he had done nothing wrong. But before he could finish speaking, the officer cut him off and began yelling at him. Rohan recalls feeling a wave of guilt wash over him, as if he must have somehow deserved this treatment. When he catches a whiff of something burning, even years later, Rohan is instantly transported back to that moment. The smell triggers a flood of memories, including the officer's angry face and the feeling of helplessness that followed. He can't shake the sense that people in uniform are inherently untrustworthy - that they're just waiting for an excuse to pounce. As a result, Rohan has become hypervigilant around anyone who looks like they might be in authority, constantly scanning their surroundings for potential threats. Rohan's difficulty articulating what happened that day is another source of distress. He knows what occurred, but whenever he tries to put it into words, the memories feel jumbled and unclear. This has led him to rehearse conversations in his head before any interaction, hoping to avoid feeling tongue-tied or defensive. Avoiding future plans has also become a habit - why make commitments when the world is just waiting to let you down? When Rohan does try to explain what happened, he often feels like he's losing the thread and can't finish. As time passes, these patterns of thought have only intensified. Rohan has come to believe that people are inherently untrustworthy, and that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place. He feels betrayed by the very system that's supposed to protect him - after all, who else was there to turn to when he needed help? This sense of betrayal fuels his hypervigilance, making it harder for him to distinguish between real threats and imagined ones. Lately, Rohan has noticed that even his work as a graphic designer is being affected. He used to love brainstorming with colleagues, but now the mere presence of authority figures in the office makes him anxious. His avoidance behaviors have started to take a toll on his relationships - his wife feels like he's pushing her away, and friends are starting to notice that Rohan never wants to make plans anymore. Rohan knows this can't go on forever. He's hoping therapy will help him untangle these knotted thoughts and feelings, and maybe - just maybe - learn to trust again. But for now, the smell of burnt rubber still sends a shiver down his spine, transporting him back to that fateful day when everything changed.
